name: The Chronicle
summary: A note on the book you are holding: who writes it, why they write it, and what an empty page in it actually means.
body: A word about this book, since you are already in it.

The Chronicle is the work of the Chroniclers, who hold that a thing written down exactly is a thing saved exactly, and who have been setting Nangijala down page by page for a long time now. Every creature described here was gone and looked at by somebody. Every account of the ages was assembled out of what people at fires could still be got to say. It is not a story anybody made up. It is a record, kept badly at the edges and very well in the middle, by people who took it seriously.
They are, it should be said, not universally loved for it. The tellers hold that a written thing stops growing, and they are not wrong. There is a stiffness to a page that there is not to an evening.

But consider what the alternative has cost. There are districts of this world that were held up for centuries by three people who were good at talking, and when those three thinned, the district went, and there is now nothing there but good grazing and a name nobody can source. The Chronicle exists because somebody looked at that and decided they would rather have a stiff and complete account of a place than a warm and vanished one.
So: read it, and treat what it says as true, because it was checked.

And when you find a page with nothing on it — a creature with no account, a place with no history, a name with no person attached — understand what you are looking at. It does not mean that nothing is known. It means no chronicler has got there yet. There are a great many more things in Nangijala than there are people willing to sit down and write about them, and the gap has been widening for some time.
If you know something that is not in here, the Chroniclers would like to hear it. That is not a formality. It is very nearly the entire method.
